lesson.title: Measuring Distance from Zero
lesson.summary: Introduces absolute value as the distance a number sits from zero on the number line, showing why that distance is always non-negative.
lesson.body:
You already know that numbers live on a number line, stretching in both directions from zero. Positive numbers sit to the right, negative numbers sit to the left, and zero sits right in the middle. Now ask a slightly different question: forget which direction a number points, and just ask how far it sits from zero. That distance ,  always measured as a plain, non-negative amount ,  is what mathematicians call the absolute value of the number.

Think about why direction shouldn't matter here. If you walk 4 steps east or 4 steps west, the distance you've traveled is the same: 4 steps. The direction changes where you end up, but not how far you went. Numbers work the same way on the line. The number 4 is 4 units from zero, and the number -4 is also 4 units from zero, just on the opposite side. Absolute value strips away the "which side" information and keeps only the "how far" information. That's why the result is never negative ,  distance itself is never a negative quantity, even when the number you started with was negative.

The notation for absolute value is a pair of vertical bars around the number, like |x|. So |-5| = 5, because -5 sits exactly 5 units to the left of zero, and the distance is 5, not -5. Likewise |5| = 5, since 5 is already 5 units to the right of zero. Notice something important: a positive number and its negative counterpart end up with the same absolute value. |7| = 7 and |-7| = 7, because both 7 and -7 are 7 units away from zero, just in opposite directions. This is the core mechanism to hold onto: absolute value doesn't care about sign at all, only about magnitude.

There's one special case worth pinning down: |0| = 0. Zero is zero units from itself, so its absolute value is zero ,  it's the only number whose absolute value is also zero, since every other number, positive or negative, sits some nonzero distance away from the origin.

You can build a simple rule from this idea without memorizing a list of examples. If the number inside the bars is positive or zero, its absolute value is just the number itself, since it's already non-negative. If the number inside the bars is negative, its absolute value is the opposite of that number ,  flipping the sign turns a negative distance-like value into the actual positive distance it represents. For instance, take -12: it's negative, so its absolute value is the opposite of -12, which is 12. Check it against the number line picture: -12 is 12 units from zero, confirming |-12| = 12.

This idea of "size regardless of direction" will keep showing up as you move deeper into algebra, especially anytime you need to talk about how far apart two numbers are, or how much something has changed without worrying about whether that change was an increase or a decrease. For now, the key habit to build is this: whenever you see the bars |...|, picture the number line, locate the number, and count how far it sits from zero ,  that count, always zero or positive, is the absolute value.
